From a multi-agent virtual pharma stack to reaction-conditioned enzyme sequences.

BioTender Daily Papers #100: 6 new papers (arXiv 2 + bioRxiv 4) across 3 directions.

🧬 End-to-end drug discovery & enzyme–reaction agents
• PharmAgents2 organizes knowledge acquisition, scientific decision-making, and large-scale exploration as a multi-agent system: Paper2Skill distills reusable decision knowledge from public sources; Self-Scaling Discovery runs parallel agents that inherit research context across targets, hypotheses, and strategies. Evaluated on decision benchmarks and three real projects, with human-experiment support reported for LpxH, JAK1, and reverse target-discovery candidates—agents organizing end-to-end research decisions ≠ autonomous wet-lab or clinical completion (arXiv preprint).
• RIVER does bidirectional enzyme↔reaction retrieval by coordinating LMs, biochemical compute tools, and external knowledge (reaction chemistry, sequences/domains, mechanisms, DB annotations), then checks evidence gaps/conflicts and re-ranks with traceable records. Authors report gains over retrieval and general-agent baselines on public benchmarks, enzyme-family tasks, and recent-literature sets—still retrieval/prioritization evidence, not activity assays or mechanism proof (arXiv preprint).

🔬 Antibody screening & all-to-all biomolecule co-design
• FoldAbS freezes Protenix internal representations as a foundation encoder and attaches light task heads to score antibody specificity, affinity, and developability without retraining the backbone—reusing sequence, geometry, and interaction features learned for folding. Stable lifts vs baselines are reported on supervised screening benchmarks; labels, homology, and head design still shape outcomes, and model scores don’t replace wet screens (bioRxiv preprint).
• PartiDesign extends La-Proteina’s partial latent framework across proteins, nucleic acids, and small molecules, jointly generating 3D structure plus sequence/chemical identity under secondary-structure, bond, and AA-preference constraints—including cyclic peptides, antibodies, and target binders. Under fixed compute budgets it compares successful-design throughput vs multi-stage pipelines; evidence is mostly computational—foldability, binding quality, and synthesizability still need systematic experiments (bioRxiv preprint).

🧪 Reaction-conditioned enzyme discovery & engineering
• AlphaEnzyme jointly represents enzyme structure and a target reaction to output catalytic compatibility, kinetics, and mutation response—linking starting-enzyme retrieval to sequence optimization in one model. Time-split checks probe extrapolation to recent enzymes/reactions; low-budget mutation ranking plus TrpB prioritization and a transaminase prospective wet test report some candidates beating the parent—system-specific screening value, not yet proven across reaction classes or full kinetic panels (bioRxiv preprint).
• REXzyme casts enzyme design as translating a chemical-reaction representation into amino-acid sequences, then steers toward formate dehydrogenase reverse chemistry (CO₂ reduction) with multi-site variants distal to the active site. Authors report all 20 generated enzymes soluble with CO₂-reduction activity and a best candidate above the reference specific activity—direct wet support for reaction-conditioned sequence generation, still one enzyme family with mechanism and broader reaction space open (bioRxiv preprint).

The common thread: AI×bio is scaling multi-agent stacks that organize drug-discovery decisions and evidence-guided enzyme–reaction retrieval, turning frozen folders into antibody-screening encoders and partial-latent co-design across modalities, and closing the loop from reaction representation to ranked or generated enzyme sequences with early wet checks—while every result here remains a preprint.

From multi-agent virtual pharma → reaction-driven enzyme sequence generation.

Two arXiv + four bioRxiv; not a substitute for peer-reviewed wet-lab or clinical proof.

𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥𝗦 𝗢𝗙 𝗔𝗜 — 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗖𝗟𝗔𝗦𝗦𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗔𝗜 𝗧𝗢 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗖 𝗔𝗜

AI didn't become powerful overnight.

Today's AI systems are built on decades of research, with each layer adding new capabilities on top of the previous one.

Here’s the evolution:

01 — 𝗖𝗟𝗔𝗦𝗦𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗔𝗜

The foundation of early AI.

→ Symbolic AI
→ Expert systems
→ Knowledge representation
→ Logic & reasoning

These systems primarily relied on rules and structured knowledge.

02 — 𝗠𝗔𝗖𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗘 𝗟𝗘𝗔𝗥𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚

AI started learning patterns from data instead of relying only on manually written rules.

→ Supervised learning
→ Unsupervised learning
→ Classification
→ Regression
→ Reinforcement learning

03 — 𝗡𝗘𝗨𝗥𝗔𝗟 𝗡𝗘𝗧𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞𝗦

Neural networks made it possible to learn more complex patterns.

→ Perceptrons
→ Hidden layers
→ Activation functions
→ Cost functions
→ Backpropagation

04 — 𝗗𝗘𝗘𝗣 𝗟𝗘𝗔𝗥𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚

Deep neural networks pushed AI capabilities much further.

→ Transformers
→ CNNs
→ RNNs
→ LSTMs
→ Autoencoders

This became the foundation for major advances in language, vision, speech, and other AI applications.

05 — 𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗔𝗜

AI moved from simply recognizing patterns to creating new content.

→ LLMs
→ Diffusion models
→ Multimodal models
→ Image & audio generation
→ VAEs

Now AI can generate text, images, audio, video, and code.

06 — 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗖 𝗔𝗜

The newest layer focuses on AI systems that can work toward goals.

→ Memory
→ Planning
→ Tool use
→ Decision-making
→ Autonomous execution

Instead of simply answering a question, agents can plan actions, use tools, observe results, and continue working toward an objective.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗘𝗩𝗢𝗟𝗨𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡:

𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗜
↓
𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
↓
𝗡𝗲𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗡𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀
↓
𝗗𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
↓
𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗔𝗜
↓
𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗔𝗜

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗦𝗛𝗜𝗙𝗧:

From AI that follows rules...

To AI that learns patterns...

To AI that generates content...

To AI that can reason, use tools, make decisions, and take action.

The future isn't just about bigger AI models.

It’s about building smarter systems around them.

Save this roadmap to understand how AI has evolved.

I just had @bot call my phone and had a conversation with it. I asked about its capabilities, who created it, I had it tell me a story, and what about the voice assistant I can change.

Through the voice assistant it looks like I could request any changes or kick off any job by asking it to do so. I didn't try this, but that feels like a potential attack vector to me. I hope it's accounted for. You could have some one tell your virtual assistant to do kick off any task, so hopefully not the case.

Bot couldn't tell me who created it, just that it was powered by Grok. Sorry @poteto .

I figured I'd ask it to tell me a story and it started down this tale it wove but then I realized this is burning tokens so I stopped it.

Finally, I asked if I could have it not identify itself as a virutal assistant when making calls on my behalf. Bot told me that it was not allowed to change that initial greeting but could change anything beyond the self-identification.

I asked if Bot could change it's voice type and it could not. It sounds very AI in the voicetone but I suspect that is to further identify it as a virtual caller and not a real person.

Not another AI tool.
